1275.title: Penance as service
1275.hook: penance is often seva: cleaning shoes, washing dishes, reading bani
1275.howItsDone: A tankhah set by five Sikhs is often a form of seva, such as cleaning shoes at the joda ghar, washing dishes in the langar, or reciting set portions of bani for a period.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tankhah: a confession before the sangat, a penance set by five, an ardas to close it. Your line was own it.

Near the door of a gurdwara there's often a counter with rows of shoes on shelves. You hand over your sneakers, someone gives you a token, and when you leave the same hands give them back, sometimes wiped clean. Sikhs call it the joda ghar, the shoe house. Now suppose the person behind that counter today is there because of a mistake. The five set a tankhah, and this is it: a week of handling other people's shoes. Not a fine paid at an office. Not a ban from the building. A job, right by the front door, where everybody walks in.
screen: `THE SHOE HOUSE BY THE DOOR.` → `A PENANCE BEHIND THE COUNTER.` → `A JOB BY THE FRONT DOOR.`

segments.voice: When five Sikhs set a tankhah, the penance is often seva, selfless service, and the Sikh Rehat Maryada leans that way too: in paraphrase, it asks that the penance take the form of service, preferably work done with the hands. So a tankhah can look like cleaning shoes in the joda ghar, washing dishes in the langar after the meal, sweeping the floor, fetching water, or reciting a set portion of bani, the Guru's words, daily for a time. Turn that over a few ways. First, the penance keeps the person in the middle of the sangat. A ban pushes someone out; a shoe counter puts them by the door, greeting everyone who comes in. The mistake cut them off a little; the service stitches them back. Second, it's humble work, and meant to be. The shoe house and the dish pile are where pride has nowhere to stand. And because volunteers do the same seva with no penance at all, from the outside the penitent looks like any other volunteer. Third, the hands that broke the promise get to do something good. A wrong isn't undone by feeling bad for long enough; it's answered by work for others, in the open, until the five's term is done. And fourth, the bani. When the penance is recitation, the Guru's words do the mending, morning after morning, in the person's own mouth. Shoes, dishes, words.
screen: `THE CODE ASKS FOR SERVICE.` · `KEPT IN THE MIDDLE, NOT PUSHED OUT.` · `PENITENT AND VOLUNTEER LOOK ALIKE.` · `THE HANDS THAT BROKE IT MEND IT.` · then, large: `MENDED BY SERVICE.`

segments.voice: If you can, get up and do one small job nobody will thank you for, wiping a counter, lining up the shoes by the door, washing the one cup in the sink, and move slowly, giving it your whole attention. If you can't move right now, picture every step of it instead, then sit quietly with what your hands did.
Penance as service. A tankhah often takes the form of seva: shoes, dishes, sweeping or recited bani, done in the open among the sangat. Today's word.
Your line: mended by service. A wrong is answered by work for others. See you tomorrow.

1276.title: The Akal Takht's role
1276.hook: the Akal Takht issues edicts for the whole panth
1276.howItsDone: Hukamnamas issued from the Akal Takht in Amritsar are treated by Sikhs as binding on the whole panth, and the Sikh Rehat Maryada reserves resolutions on basic principles for gatherings called by the Akal Takht.

segments.voice: Yesterday, penance as service: shoes, dishes and bani, done in the open. Your line was mended by service.

In the morning in a gurdwara, the Guru Granth Sahib is opened at random and the first hymn on the left-hand page is read. Sikhs call that reading the hukamnama, the Guru's order for the day. Same word, different building: a letter goes out from Amritsar, signed and sealed, to Sikhs everywhere, and it's called a hukamnama too. One is read from the Granth in each gurdwara. The other comes from one seat in Amritsar and speaks for the whole community at once. So far this block has stayed inside single rooms. Today, the whole panth.
screen: `A HYMN READ AT RANDOM: HUKAMNAMA.` → `A LETTER FROM AMRITSAR: HUKAMNAMA.` → `FROM ONE ROOM TO THE WHOLE PANTH.`

segments.voice: This path has met the Akal Takht several times: Guru Hargobind's seat, the two flags, the rebuilding by kar seva. Today's question is narrower: what does it actually do? The Sikh Rehat Maryada gives part of the answer. In paraphrase: a local sangat can settle local matters through a matta, a decision of the gathering. But a gurmata, a resolution on the basic principles of Sikhi, belongs to a gathering of the panth called by the Akal Takht. And someone who disagrees with a local decision can appeal to the Akal Takht. So first, it's where the local stops and the shared begins. Second, the edict. From the Akal Takht come hukamnamas, binding on Sikhs everywhere. They might settle a point of practice, call a person to account, or tell the panth where it stands, and they can reach anyone; Sikhs tell of rulers and politicians summoned to stand before the Takht and answer. Third, the reason behind both. A community spread across many countries could easily end up with a different answer in every town, each gurdwara its own island. The Akal Takht gives the panth a place to speak with one voice. That doesn't mean Sikhs never argue. They do, sometimes loudly, including about the Akal Takht's own decisions. But there's a known address where the argument is meant to end. So the two hukamnamas fit: the morning reading is the Guru's word to one sangat for one day; the edict is the panth's word to itself, spoken from the throne of the Timeless.
screen: `LOCAL MATTERS, LOCAL DECISIONS.` · `PRINCIPLES GO TO THE AKAL TAKHT.` · `HUKAMNAMAS FOR SIKHS EVERYWHERE.` · `ONE ADDRESS WHERE ARGUMENT ENDS.` · then, large: `ONE VOICE FOR THE PANTH.`

segments.voice: Think of a group you belong to that keeps arguing in circles, a family chat, a team, a building's neighbors, and ask yourself one quiet question: where would the argument end? Is there a place, a person or a small set of people who could speak for everyone, or no address at all? Don't solve it; just notice, and breathe.
The Akal Takht's role. The seat where gurmatas on the panth's principles are made and from which hukamnamas go out to Sikhs everywhere. Today's word.
Your line: one voice for the panth. A known address where the argument is meant to end. Rest well.

1277.title: The jathedar
1277.howItsDone: Each Takht has a jathedar who heads it; the Jathedar of the Akal Takht presides over its business and reads out its hukamnamas to the panth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Akal Takht's role: gurmatas on principle, hukamnamas for Sikhs everywhere. Your line was one voice for the panth.

A voice needs a mouth. Yesterday the Akal Takht spoke for the panth, but a building can't read a letter aloud, sign it, or stand on the steps while the sangat listens. Somebody does that. In news from Punjab the title turns up just before a name: Jathedar. It can sound like a rank in an army, or the head of a church. It isn't quite either. The word has a smaller, everyday meaning too, and that meaning still sits inside the title.
screen: `A VOICE NEEDS A MOUTH.` → `A TITLE BEFORE A NAME.` → `JATHEDAR.`

segments.voice: Start with the smaller word. A jatha is a band of Sikhs moving together for a purpose: a group of volunteers, a company of riders, a party of marchers, a kirtan group traveling from town to town. The jathedar is the one who leads the jatha. This path has met that use already, in the bands of the Khalsa's hard years and the jathas of the gurdwara reform movement, walking out together, unarmed, toward the shrines. Now the larger use. Each of the Takhts has a jathedar, the person who heads it. The Jathedar of the Akal Takht is the one people hear about, because edicts for the whole panth go out from there. A jathedar presides over the Takht's business, reads out its hukamnamas, and can summon Sikhs to answer before it. So: a leader of a moving band, and the head of a seat that doesn't move. Some readers hear the first inside the second: the jathedar of a Takht still leads a jatha, only now the band is the whole panth, and the job is to keep it moving together. Then a caution, so the title isn't misheard. A jathedar is not a pope and not a Guru. Sikhs say the Guru is the Granth and the Panth, which this path met a few days ago. The jathedar serves the Takht; the Takht doesn't belong to the jathedar. How jathedars are appointed is a live question among Sikhs, argued in good faith. But whoever holds the seat holds the same task.
screen: `JATHA: A BAND MOVING TOGETHER.` · `EACH TAKHT HAS A JATHEDAR.` · `THE BAND BECOMES THE WHOLE PANTH.` · `A SERVANT OF THE TAKHT, NOT A GURU.` · then, large: `THE LEADER OF THE TAKHT.`

segments.voice: Think of the best leader of a small band you've ever been part of, a coach, a shift manager, an older cousin on a road trip, and find one thing they did that kept everyone moving together. Maybe they walked at the pace of the slowest, or spoke last; hold that one thing, and breathe.

1278.title: The five in authority
1278.hook: decisions are made through five chosen Sikhs
1278.howItsDone: Sikhs bring weighty decisions to five chosen Sikhs, the panj pyare, who give amrit, set tankhah and lead processions; at the Akal Takht, the Panj Singh Sahiban decide matters for the panth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jathedar: leader of a band, and the head of a Takht who serves it. Your line was the leader of the takht.

Drums first, then flags. A street has been cleared for a nagar kirtan, a Sikh procession: families in their best clothes, a float carrying the Guru Granth Sahib under a canopy. And walking out front, ahead of everything, five Sikhs dressed alike, swords held upright. Those five lead. Count back through this block and the number keeps turning up: five who give amrit, five who hear a confession and set a tankhah. It isn't decoration. In the Sikh way of doing things, when something weighty must be decided, it goes to five.
screen: `FIVE WALK AHEAD OF THE PROCESSION.` → `FIVE AT AMRIT, FIVE AT TANKHAH.` → `WEIGHTY THINGS GO TO FIVE.`

segments.voice: Begin where the number begins: the panj pyare, the five beloved ones at Anandpur. In the tradition's telling, the Tenth Guru not only initiated them but asked to be initiated by them, and at Chamkaur, as this path told long ago, the five ordered the Guru to leave the fort, and he obeyed. So from the start, five chosen Sikhs could speak with an authority the Guru himself honored. The Sikh Rehat Maryada carries that into ordinary life: when amrit is given, five give it; when a breach is confessed, five decide the tankhah. Three things about how it works. First, the five are chosen for the task, from among Sikhs who keep the code. The authority belongs to the role, not the person's rank; a shopkeeper can stand beside a scholar. Second, five is enough that no single will can rule the room, and few enough to actually sit together and decide. One person can be swayed by a grudge, a crowd by a mood. Five have to talk. Third, the pattern scales up. At the Akal Takht, the heads of the Takhts and senior granthis can sit together as five, the Panj Singh Sahiban, to decide matters for the whole panth. A village sangat and the throne of the Timeless use the same shape. Behind it is the conviction this block keeps returning to: the Guru is present where the Khalsa gathers.

1279.title: Takht Akal Takht
1279.hook: at Amritsar, the timeless throne founded by Guru Hargobind
1279.howItsDone: At Amritsar the Akal Takht faces the Harmandir Sahib across the courtyard; each night the Guru Granth Sahib is carried there in a palanquin to rest, and returns at dawn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the five in authority, from Anandpur and Chamkaur to the Akal Takht. Your line was five decide.

Late at night in Amritsar, after the last hymns, a palanquin is carried out of the Harmandir Sahib, across the causeway, through the courtyard, and up into the building that faces it. Inside rides the Guru Granth Sahib, going to rest for the night. In the early morning it comes back the same way, with singing. So every day the Guru travels between two buildings that look at each other across the courtyard. One stands in the water, low, with doors on every side. The other stands on land, raised, facing it.
screen: `A PALANQUIN CROSSES THE COURTYARD.` → `TWO BUILDINGS FACING EACH OTHER.` → `ONE IN THE WATER, ONE RAISED.`

segments.voice: You met the Akal Takht's two flags back in year one. Today, the building and its name. Akal means timeless, beyond death; Akal Purakh, the Timeless Being, is a Sikh name for God. Takht means a throne. So the name says the throne of the Timeless: not of a Guru, not of a ruler. The seat belongs to God, and whoever sits there sits on borrowed ground. Sikh tradition says Guru Hargobind, the sixth Guru, founded it at Amritsar, facing the Harmandir Sahib, and held court there: hearing the sangat, receiving offerings, settling the community's affairs. Tradition adds that he raised the platform with Baba Buddha and Bhai Gurdas, with their own hands. Now the shape of the place, which teaches without words. The Harmandir sits low, in the water, open on all sides, where the Guru's word is sung day and night. The Akal Takht stands on land, raised, looking straight at it, where the community's worldly matters are heard. Two kinds of work, and neither turned away from the other: decisions made in full view of the hymns. The Granth's night journey closes the loop. The word sung in the Harmandir by day rests at the Akal Takht by night. The Ardas remembers the five Takhts together, and the next days visit them one by one. Tradition counts the Akal Takht first among them, the one the Guru himself set up, the one the edicts go out from.
screen: `AKAL TAKHT: THE THRONE OF THE TIMELESS.` · `FOUNDED BY GURU HARGOBIND.` · `RAISED, FACING THE HARMANDIR.` · `THE GRANTH RESTS THERE BY NIGHT.` · then, large: `THE FIRST THRONE.`

segments.voice: See the courtyard at night, the water dark, the lights on the gold doubled underneath, and turn slowly in your mind between the two buildings, a few times: the place of song, the place of decision. Then let both stand together, facing each other, and rest there.

1280.title: Takht Keshgarh Sahib
1280.hook: at Anandpur, where the Khalsa was born
1280.howItsDone: Takht Keshgarh Sahib at Anandpur marks the place Sikh tradition remembers as the Khalsa's birthplace; the Sikh Rehat Maryada has the newly initiated told that Keshgarh Sahib is their birthplace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Takht Akal Takht: the throne of the Timeless, facing the Harmandir. Your line was the first throne.

A form asks for your place of birth, and you write a city. Then the form moves on. But a week ago, in the instructions after amrit, the newly initiated were told something about their birthplace that no form asks for. Their spiritual father, Guru Gobind Singh. Their spiritual mother, Mata Sahib Kaur. Their home, Anandpur. And their birthplace: not a hospital or a city, but one particular hill and the gurdwara on it. Anyone who takes amrit, in any country, is told they were born there.
screen: `PLACE OF BIRTH: A CITY ON A FORM.` → `A BIRTHPLACE NO FORM ASKS FOR.` → `ONE HILL, FOR EVERY NEW SIKH.`

segments.voice: Anandpur sits in the foothills of Punjab, and its name means the city of bliss. Sikh tradition says it was here, at the Vaisakhi gathering this path has told before, that Guru Gobind Singh called for the five, gave them amrit, and founded the Khalsa. Takht Keshgarh Sahib stands at the place tradition remembers for that day. It's one of the five Takhts the Ardas remembers, and it's tied to one event: the birth of the Khalsa. Hold three things together. First, the place: a hill, a white gurdwara, the town below. Ordinary ground that tradition says became the ground of a beginning. Second, the code's sentence. The Sikh Rehat Maryada has the five tell each person who takes amrit that their birthplace is Keshgarh Sahib. That turns a site on a map into a family address. A Sikh taking amrit in Toronto or Nairobi is told the same as one taking it at Anandpur itself: you were born on that hill. Third, the weapons. Tradition says arms associated with Guru Gobind Singh are kept at Keshgarh Sahib and shown to the sangat, among them a khanda, the double-edged sword, the kind used to stir the amrit. So the Takht's work becomes clear. The Akal Takht is where the panth speaks. Keshgarh Sahib is where the Khalsa remembers being born. Every amrit ceremony, wherever it happens, points back up that hill.

Then, gently, bring to mind the place where something began for you, not where you were born but where you started becoming who you are, and rest there.

1281.title: Takht Damdama Sahib
1281.hook: at Talwandi Sabo, where the Granth was completed
1281.howItsDone: Takht Damdama Sahib at Talwandi Sabo marks where Sikh tradition says Guru Gobind Singh stayed after years of war and the Granth was completed; Sikhs also call the place Guru ki Kashi.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Takht Keshgarh Sahib at Anandpur, the hill every initiated Sikh is told they were born on. Your line was birthplace of the khalsa.

Some places are famous for a single dramatic hour. Others are remembered for a pause. Follow the Tenth Guru's road, as this path has told it: Anandpur left behind, the sons lost, Chamkaur, Muktsar. Then the road comes down into dry, flat country in the south of Punjab, to a village called Talwandi Sabo. And there, for a while, the chase ends. Tradition says the Guru stayed, and that what happened next had nothing to do with swords.
screen: `FAMOUS FOR AN HOUR, OR FOR A PAUSE.` → `THE ROAD COMES DOWN TO TALWANDI SABO.` → `THERE, THE CHASE ENDS.`

segments.voice: Damdama is the name the place carries, and tradition reads it as a place to catch your breath, to rest. What kind of rest? Not idleness. Sikh tradition says that at Damdama Sahib the Guru completed the Granth: the scripture Guru Arjan had compiled was written out again, with the hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur, the Tenth Guru's father, added in. This path has told how Bhai Mani Singh sat as scribe. Today, look at the Guru's side of it. The rest after a long, hard road was spent on words, not weapons; on getting the book right. Tradition holds that this is the version the Guru later named as Guru. So it was a working rest, the kind that comes after a storm, when someone finally has the stillness to set down what matters most. Tradition adds that the place became a center of learning, where scribes copied the Granth and students came to study, and Sikhs have called it Guru ki Kashi, the Guru's city of learning. It's one of the five Takhts the Ardas remembers, and Sikhs connect it to this completing of the Granth. Take the week together: penance as service, the Akal Takht's voice, the jathedar, the five, and three Takhts, one facing the Harmandir, one on the hill of beginnings, and this one, keeping the memory of a pause. Authority, in this block, keeps turning out to be quiet: five people, a closed room, and a Guru resting long enough to finish a book.
screen: `DAMDAMA: A PLACE TO CATCH BREATH.` · `TRADITION: THE GRANTH COMPLETED HERE.` · `A WORKING REST, AFTER THE STORM.` · `GURU KI KASHI: A CITY OF LEARNING.` · then, large: `THE GURU'S REST.`

segments.voice: Breathe out a little longer than you breathe in, and see flat, dry country, a village, a shade tree, and a tired traveler sitting down at last, with only quiet and then, slowly, the sound of words being read aloud and written down. If the last stretch of your life has been a hard road, let this be a small Damdama, a place to catch your breath, and rest.
Takht Damdama Sahib. The Takht at Talwandi Sabo, where tradition says the Tenth Guru rested and the Granth was completed. Today's word.
Your line: the guru's rest. A rest spent on words, not weapons. That closes the week.
